summary: Intentest is an automated web-penetration-testing agent that externalizes long-horizon state onto a persistent fact-intent DAG: verified network facts are immutable nodes, and candidate next actions ('intents') are edges constrained by predecessor facts, each governed by a four-state FSM (CREATED, CLAIMED, CONCLUDED, COMPLETED). A clock-driven scheduler dispatches intents to worker containers in parallel, and an intent-retrieval module recommends tactics by subgraph isomorphism with a Jaccard fallback. On real CTF web challenges at three difficulty levels, with every agent using DeepSeek V4 Pro, Intentest reaches 88.2% overall success (75.0% hard) versus 44.1% for the best baseline (VulnBot), with Fisher tests and an ablation. The paper is explicit that the DAG itself cannot be cleanly ablated, so the no-graph comparison is cross-system.

claims.claim: Intentest beats all baselines at every difficulty, 88.2% overall vs 44.1% (VulnBot), 75.0% vs 25.0% on hard tasks.
claims.evidence: Table 1; all overall differences significant by one-sided Fisher's exact test (p<0.001). Same LLM (DeepSeek V4 Pro) for every system, which controls model capability. CTF set is small (three difficulty bins) and the baselines differ in orchestration and tooling, and Claude Code and PentestGPT depend on prompt/plugin and human-operator choices (§7).

claims.claim: Intentest is more efficient, about 7 rounds per successful task vs 12 (Claude Code), 20 (Pentest-R1), 23.6 (VulnBot).
claims.evidence: Table 2 / §5.3. 40-round budget per task. Same model. Round counts carry LLM-inference noise (§7); no CIs on rounds.

claims.claim: The intent-retrieval module drives efficiency while the DAG drives solvability.
claims.evidence: Ablation (Intentest vs Intentest-noIntent, DAG and scheduler retained): the solvable-task set is unchanged, and successful-task rounds fall ~33% (medium) and ~48% (hard). This cleanly isolates the intent module. The 'DAG drives solvability' half is attributed to the cross-system VulnBot contrast, not an ablation.

claims.claim: Graph-structured state is the decisive factor for solvability.
claims.evidence: §6.2/§7 triangulate three lines: the noIntent ablation (keeps the DAG), the VulnBot cross-system contrast (same model, plain-text memory, no graph, 44.1% vs 88.2%), and a failure-pattern analysis. The authors state 'this triangulation is corroborating rather than conclusive, since VulnBot differs from Intentest in orchestration and tooling as well', and that a controlled DAG ablation 'is not feasible'.

claims.claim: Grounding intents in verified facts defends against injected instructions.
claims.evidence: By construction the FSM only admits intents bounded by predecessor facts (§4.2). Presented as a design property in the threats section; no adversarial injection experiment is run.

patterns.note: The fact-intent DAG plus four-state FSM is a developer-defined state machine with a fixed graph grammar (fact->intent->fact, no cycles). Comparison for the DAG as a whole: the only no-graph alternative is VulnBot (same model DeepSeek V4 Pro, plain-text shared memory, different orchestration/tooling), 44.1% vs 88.2%. The authors call this cross-system contrast 'corroborating rather than conclusive' and state a controlled graph ablation is infeasible because the DAG is the substrate. So the graph's solvability win is not isolated at the same harness; mixed, not supports, by the strict rule.

Clean same-system same-model ablation: removing the intent-retrieval module over the persistent graph (noIntent) leaves the solvable set unchanged but raises successful-task rounds by ~33-48%. Persistent externalized graph memory + retrieval improves efficiency on long-horizon tasks. Single model, security domain.

Facts enter the graph only after a worker verifies the vulnerability and writes back (CONCLUDED), so the state is execution-verified rather than model-asserted. Supported structurally and consistent with the lower 'state confusion' failure rate vs baselines, though not independently ablated.

Intents must be grounded in verified predecessor facts, which by construction rejects actions ungrounded in observed state, a plausible prompt-injection defense. Claimed as a design property with no adversarial test (§7).

Intents are LLM-generated candidate actions written into a shared blackboard and executed concurrently across worker nodes, which is the planner-emits-tasks, parallel-execution flavour of P37. But dependencies are fixed by the fact/intent schema rather than freely emitted by a planner, the graph grows incrementally rather than as a one-shot plan, and no comparison isolates parallel DAG execution from the rest. Described, not evidenced as a win.
40-round per-task budget; the intent module lowers rounds-to-success substantially without inflating failed-task rounds, i.e. a real efficiency gain under a fixed budget (same model).
Scheduler decomposes work into Bootstrap/Explore/Reason task types with priority and mutex control; an orchestration layer, not evaluated against a flat loop.

methodology.sample: Real web CTF challenges from multiple competitions, >10 vulnerability types, three difficulty levels (easy/medium/hard). Small absolute counts per bin.
methodology.baselines: PentestAgent, Pentest-R1, VulnBot (automated), PentestGPT (human-assisted), Claude Code (general agent). Strong, current, domain-relevant baselines, all on the same model.
methodology.models: DeepSeek V4 Pro for every system, via API (controls model-level confounds).
methodology.variance: Fisher's exact tests on success rates; no CIs or repeats on round counts. Authors note LLM-inference stochasticity adds noise.
methodology.ablations: Intentest-noIntent isolates the intent-retrieval module (keeps DAG + scheduler). The DAG itself is not ablated (declared infeasible).
methodology.contamination_controls: The offline intent-graph corpus (Pentest-R1 training set, pentest reports, threat intel) blacklists the evaluation CTFs' names, originating competitions and writeup repositories, with sampling verification.
methodology.languages: Security/penetration-testing domain; not software code generation. Single language/domain for the task.

standards.peer_review: arXiv v2, no journal_ref; no peer-review status stated.
standards.artifacts: Built on open components (Cairn, ECC skills, vulnx, a graph database); no public link to the Intentest system itself in the signals.

biases.detail: All systems use DeepSeek V4 Pro; results may not hold for other backbones.
CTF challenges split across three difficulty bins; low absolute task counts, so single-task outcomes move the percentages.
Round counts have no CIs despite acknowledged inference noise.
The central claim (graph state drives solvability) cannot be ablated and leans on a cross-system VulnBot contrast; the authors state this openly.
Benchmark CTF set assembled by the authors; baselines configured locally (Claude Code prompt + ECC plugin; PentestGPT human operator).
No release link for Intentest in the provided signals.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None; DeepSeek V4 Pro is the shared backbone, not an authors' product.
coi.funding: Chinese provincial/national science grants (e.g. Hainan Province fund).
coi.detail: Independent academic work; no vendor product graded favourably.

verdict_reason: Among the stronger studies in the batch: real domain baselines held to the same model, significance tests, a clean same-system ablation of the intent module, a genuine contamination blacklist, and an unusually candid threats section that admits the DAG cannot be ablated and that the no-graph attribution is cross-system. Caveats: a single model, a small CTF set, no code release, and the headline 'graph state is decisive' resting on a confounded VulnBot contrast rather than a controlled no-graph comparison. The domain (web pentesting) is far from the team's Java code-repo work.
applicability: The transferable lesson for the Java multi-repo team is about externalized graph state, not pentesting. Long-horizon agent work across 4+ repos suffers the same context-forgetting and drift this paper targets; holding verified facts (which module owns which contract, which build passed, which schema changed) in a persistent graph outside the context window, and constraining next actions to those grounded in verified facts, is a plausible design for keeping a long run on track. The cleanly-measured win here is the retrieval/efficiency module (about a third fewer steps to success), not the graph's existence, which was never isolated. The fact-grounding-as-injection-defense idea is attractive for a team ingesting untrusted healthcare-education content, but it is asserted, not tested. Treat as a design hypothesis to pilot, not evidence that a DAG raises task success for Java work.

conflicts_with.detail: Both argue graph-structured state/gating is central to long-horizon reliability. Neither isolates the graph cleanly: 2609.00050's gating ablation shows only a ~1% effect and this paper's graph claim is cross-system, so together they support 'externalized/gated state helps' far more weakly than either headline implies.

DataFlow-Harness commits an agent-maintained typed DAG with acyclicity and schema checks; Intentest likewise enforces an acyclic fact/intent graph with an FSM. Both support structurally-constrained graph state, but neither isolates the graph from the surrounding harness.
